title: [rtl] Change how we record debug causes
body:
This commit changes when we catch the debug causes. Since `debug_cause_o` only gets saved when `csr_save_cause_o` is high, it would work if we change the cause with a mux that is connected to the input signals.

Resolves #1772

Signed-off-by: Canberk Topal <ctopal@lowrisc.org>

repo.name: ibex
repo.description: Ibex is a small 32 bit RISC-V CPU core, previously known as zero-riscy.

Resolves #1772

resolved_issues.title: Cosim mismatch when reading DCSR.cause
resolved_issues.body:
## Observed Behavior
Test failures with the following error : 
```
UVM_FATAL ibex_cosim_scoreboard.sv(138) @ 4049807: Cosim mismatch Register write data mismatch to x22 DUT: 40000100 expected: 400000c0
```

This fails upon reading from `DCSR.cause`
In this case : 

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/102029880/184605611-4f106a6b-a987-4952-b636-760647e12afe.png)
(IBEX)

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/102029880/184605563-b1bd1eb8-b8c3-47c2-b263-3c84427153f3.png)
(SPIKE)

Observing the waveform below, we can see that `debug_req_i` is de-asserted shortly after `debug_mode_i` goes low due to leaving debug mode from a dret. We do re-enter debug mode, but the cause can be seen to be recorded as `DBG_CAUSE_STEP`. In spike, we read back `DBG_CAUSE_HALTREQ` at the same instruction, hence the mismatch.

## Expected Behavior

Ibex should record `DCSR.cause` as DBG_CAUSE_HALTREQ.

I think this might be due to the [ibex_controller.sv ](https://github.com/lowRISC/ibex/blob/2f8dfa9dfe2d938228118ed8ab6a543804d0c9ae/rtl/ibex_controller.sv#L662)state machine sampling the `debug_req_i` signal to determine the correct `cause` one cycle later than the decision to enter debug_mode.

## Steps to reproduce the issue
```
cd dv/uvm/core_ibex/
make TEST=riscv_debug_basic_test ITERATIONS=1 WAVES=1 SEED=9892 -j12 -ik
```
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/102029880/184603232-ef1a9397-1cd2-4a0b-828b-1b2eb4e1745a.png)

> estimate 8
> remaining 2022-09-27 4
> remaining 2022-10-12 1

#!/bin/bash
set -euxo pipefail

cd /home/ibex
git checkout -- .
git clean -fdx
git checkout 70186c57aeff46ff47b80e8f3d6e2c3d849f2e5b
git submodule sync --recursive
git submodule update --init --recursive
apt-get update
DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive apt-get install -y verilator
echo 'export PATH=/usr/bin:$PATH' > /etc/profile.d/ibex-verilator.sh
. /etc/profile.d/ibex-verilator.sh
git rev-parse HEAD > /tmp/ibex_baseline_commit
problem_statement: Reading the `cause` field of the RISC-V Debug Control and Status Register (`DCSR.cause`) can report the wrong reason for entering debug mode. In the failing behavior, Ibex records a single-step cause (`DBG_CAUSE_STEP`) even though debug mode was entered because of an external debug request (`debug_req_i`), which should be reported as `DBG_CAUSE_HALTREQ`. This affects the debug-entry cause recording logic in `ibex_controller`. The bug is triggered when the core decides to enter debug mode because `debug_req_i` is asserted, but `debug_req_i` is de-asserted before the later cycle that saves the cause into `DCSR.cause`; the issue was observed after a debug return instruction (`dret`) followed by immediate re-entry into debug mode. In that situation, `DCSR.cause` must still read back as `DBG_CAUSE_HALTREQ`, because the debug entry was caused by the halt request rather than by single-step execution.

title: [rtl] Do not register instruction fetch errors
body:
Registering instruction fetch errors causes problem in the case of seeing
a PMP execution access block. ID/EX stage learns about
the instruction that it executed should be blocked a
cycle late. This commit fixes that.

Found this one while working on fixing https://github.com/lowRISC/ibex/issues/1720. However it does not fully solves the issue because we are still seeing some mismatches because of some self modifying code problems.

Signed-off-by: Canberk Topal <ctopal@lowrisc.org>

repo.name: ibex
repo.description: Ibex is a small 32 bit RISC-V CPU core, previously known as zero-riscy.

commits.message:
[rtl] Flush controller in PMP CSR write ops

As Greg pointed out:

When we have an instruction in ID/EX that writes a PMP register that
update gets written to the CSR the same cycle the next instruction
moves from IF to ID/EX with it's PMP check done with the old value.

The solution is to flush the pipeline when we get a PMP CSR write.

Signed-off-by: Canberk Topal <ctopal@lowrisc.org>

#!/bin/bash
cd /home/ibex
set -uo pipefail
set +e

TEST_NAME="pmp_ifetch_flush"
TB_DIR="/home/ibex/.tb_${TEST_NAME}"
SIM_LOG="/home/ibex/${TEST_NAME}_sim.log"
SW_LOG="/home/ibex/${TEST_NAME}_sw_build.log"
RUNTIME_LOG="/home/ibex/ibex_simple_system.log"
SIM_BIN="/home/ibex/build/lowrisc_ibex_ibex_simple_system_0/sim-verilator/Vibex_simple_system"

finish_test() {
  local status="$1"
  local exit_code="$2"

  echo "HWE_BENCH_RESULTS_START"
  echo "TEST: ${TEST_NAME} ... ${status}"
  echo "HWE_BENCH_RESULTS_END"
  exit "${exit_code}"
}

rm -rf "${TB_DIR}"
mkdir -p "${TB_DIR}"

cat > "${TB_DIR}/Makefile" <<'EOF'
PROGRAM = pmp_ifetch_flush
PROGRAM_DIR := $(shell dirname $(realpath $(lastword $(MAKEFILE_LIST))))
EXTRA_SRCS := $(PROGRAM_DIR)/test_main.S
include /home/ibex/examples/sw/simple_system/common/common.mk
EOF

cat > "${TB_DIR}/pmp_ifetch_flush.c" <<'EOF'
/* Intentionally empty: main is implemented in pmp_ifetch_flush.S. */
EOF

cat > "${TB_DIR}/test_main.S" <<'EOF'
// Copyright lowRISC contributors.
// Licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0, see LICENSE for details.
// SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0

  .section .text
  .globl main
  .option norvc

main:
  la   a0, blocked_insn
  srli a0, a0, 2
  csrw pmpaddr0, a0
  li   a0, 0x90
  csrw pmpcfg0, a0

blocked_insn:
  j    after_blocked

after_blocked:
  la   a0, no_trap_msg
  call puts
  call sim_halt
1:
  j    1b

  .section .rodata
no_trap_msg:
  .asciz "NO_TRAP\n"
EOF

make -C "${TB_DIR}" CC=riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc ARCH=rv32im > "${SW_LOG}" 2>&1
sw_rc=$?
cat "${SW_LOG}"
if [ ${sw_rc} -ne 0 ]; then
  finish_test "FAIL" "${sw_rc}"
fi

python3 - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path

path = Path("/home/ibex/examples/simple_system/ibex_simple_system.cc")
text = path.read_text()
old = """std::string SimpleSystem::GetIsaString() const {
  const Vibex_simple_system &top = _top;
  assert(top.ibex_simple_system);

problem_statement: Ibex can apply a Physical Memory Protection (PMP) update one instruction late. When software writes a PMP address or configuration CSR so that the next instruction address becomes non-executable, the core may still fetch that next instruction and let it execute instead of faulting immediately. The expected behavior is that the updated PMP permissions take effect for the very next instruction fetch: if the next program counter is now blocked for execution, that instruction must not execute and the core must raise an instruction access fault at that program counter. This bug affects PMP-based instruction-fetch permission checking, and it is triggered by a PMP CSR write immediately followed by a fetch from the newly blocked address.

title: Move not-taken, predicted taken branch address calculation to ID stage
body:
Currently, the not-taken address of a branch is registered in flops in the prefetch buffer or instruction cache when ever a branch prediction is lodged with these modules. However, as discussed in https://github.com/lowRISC/ibex/issues/1462, there is an issue with this address being overridden by a second predicted branch when the an instruction moves from the prefetch to the IF stage skid buffer. If the instruction in the skid buffer was mispredicted taken, the prefetch will replay from the stored address of the second predicted branch, not the first one.

To solve this without adding extra flops in the IF stage to store the not-taken address of the instruction in the skid buffer, we can get rid of these flops entirely and calculate the not-taken address in the ID stage. This would be fed back along with the existing not-taken mispredict signal `nt_branch_mispredict_i` used to clear the prefetch and allows it to resume fetching on the correct path.

As a code refactoring bonus, we do not need to consider the existence of the branch predictor in the prefetch buffer, instruction cache and fetch FIFO modules any more. Previously, the next address of the fetch FIFO would be registered in flops as the not-taken address using an `if generate` block based on the `BranchPredictor` parameter, but these flops do not exist anymore as of this PR.

Though not specifically relevant to this change, we now also suppress the validity of the skid buffer content by `nt_branch_mispredict_i` which prevents mispredicted instructions in the skid buffer from entering the ID stage. This is required as part of fixing the aforementioned bug.

resolved_issues.body:
<!--
Thank you for your interest in Ibex. We are continuously improving Ibex, and your bug report will help us with that. To help us understand and reproduce your problem as quickly as possible we have prepared a little template below.

No text in blocks starting with < !-- will be shown in the final bug report.

You can also copy/paste images into the bug report, and you can attach files to it by simply dragging them into the issue window.
-->

## Steps to reproduce the issue
<!--
Please help us to reproduce the issue you're seeing by including a detailed description of what you did to get to the problem.

For example:
* What command did you run? (Also include the output of the command.)
* What parameters/defines did you set?
* Did you make modifications to the source code?
-->
Consider the following code:
```
int main(int argc, char **argv) {
    static int x = 25;
    int* x_addr = (int*)&x;
    __asm__ (
        "j skip\n\t"

        "predict_to_here:\n\t" // we shouldn't branch here but even if we do, just finish
        "j finish\n\t"
        "wfi\n\t" // this will kill things if hit

        "skip:\n\t"
        "lw t0, 0(%0)\n\t"
        "beqz t0, predict_to_here\n\t" // clearly this branch is not meant to be taken but is predicted taken
        "j finish\n\t"

        "finish:\n\t"
        "nop\n\t"
        :
        :"r" (x_addr)
        : "t0"
    );
    return 0;

}
```
We would expect the following branch pattern in general: `-> skip -> finish`
Building ibex_simple_system with the following parameters works correctly:
`fusesoc --cores-root=. run --target=sim --setup --build lowrisc:ibex:ibex_simple_system --RV32E=0 --RV32M=ibex_pkg::RV32MFast --BranchTargetALU=1 --WritebackStage=1 --BranchPredictor=0`

Building with these parameters causes the core to seemingly "lock up":
`fusesoc --cores-root=. run --target=sim --setup --build lowrisc:ibex:ibex_simple_system --RV32E=0 --RV32M=ibex_pkg::RV32MFast --BranchTargetALU=1 --WritebackStage=1 --BranchPredictor=1`

## Observed Behavior
<!--
Please describe the problem you saw. Include waveforms (in VCD or Verilator/GtkWave FST format only please) and log files if possible.
-->
Ibex overrides `branch_mispredict_addr` by predicting on a predicted branch. This means when a mispredict fires on `beqz t0, predict_to_here` the PC fetched next is at `wfi`.

[waves.zip](https://github.com/lowRISC/ibex/files/7384667/waves.zip)

## Expected Behavior
<!-- Please describe the behavior you expected to see instead. -->
I honestly don't know. In the prefetch buffer configuration, there is only one `branch_mispredict_addr_q` present so there is no practical way to nest branch predictions as far as I can tell. It seems like branches should just be predicted not taken when we are already on a predicted path.

## My Environment

<!--
Let us know how you're using Ibex. This helps us to better understand your problem and find a solution more quickly.
-->
**Compiler:**
riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc (GCC) 8.2.0

**EDA tool and version:**
<!--
If you are using an EDA tool to work with Ibex let us know which tool and which version you're using.
For example, "Xilinx Vivado 2020.1" or "Synopsys VCS 2020.03-SP1"
-->
Verilator 4.210 2021-07-07 rev v4.210

**Operating system:**
<!--
Please let us know the operating system/Linux distribution you're using.
For example "Ubuntu Linux 18.04" or "CentOS 7.3".
-->
Ubuntu 21.04

**Version of the Ibex source code:**
<!--
Which version of the Ibex source code are you using?
You can call `git rev-parse HEAD` in your Ibex source directory to get this information.
Please also let us know if you have made changes to the code.
-->
cfeef7e864926cf4d30e271a3e2aa5d95e0c141f

problem_statement: When `BranchPredictor=1`, Ibex can mis-handle recovery from a branch that was predicted taken but later resolves as not taken if that branch is still unresolved while fetch continues down the predicted path. In the reported failing case, a preceding load delays resolution of the first branch, a later branch or jump on the speculative path is also predicted, and the recovery state for the earlier branch is replaced by the later prediction. Instructions from the wrong path can also remain buffered in the instruction fetch pipeline. When the earlier branch is finally resolved as not taken, the core can resume from the wrong PC and continue with wrong-path instructions, which can send execution into an unintended instruction stream and make the core appear to lock up. The expected behavior is that a predicted-taken branch that resolves as not taken must restart execution from the instruction immediately following that branch, independent of any later predictions, and any buffered instructions from the wrong predicted path must be discarded. This affects the instruction-fetch branch prediction and not-taken mispredict recovery logic.

title: [rtl] Various security feature bugfixes
body:
- Document that SecureIbex cannot be used without a multiplier and add
  an assertion in the rtl. This fixes #1080.
- Move the PC checking hardware onto its own parameter to match all the
  other individual security features.
- Make the PC increment behavior more sensible on fetch errors (and make
  it match the icache behavior). Factor this into the PC increment check
  to prevent false triggering, fixes #1094.
- Stop the PC mismatch checker firing on dummy instructions, fixes
  #1095.

Signed-off-by: Tom Roberts <tomroberts@lowrisc.org>

problem_statement: An instruction bus error in the Ibex instruction-fetch path can be misclassified when it occurs on a 32-bit instruction that starts at a half-word-aligned address, so the instruction spans two 16-bit halves across fetch words. In that case, the fetch logic may treat the faulting instruction as if the first half were a completed 16-bit RISC-V compressed instruction, advance the instruction stream by 2 bytes, and, when SecureIbex's sequential program-counter check is enabled, raise a spurious PC mismatch alarm. The correct behavior is that a fetch error must not cause that unaligned 32-bit instruction to be treated as compressed: the instruction must remain incomplete until both halves are available, and the next sequential PC tracked by the fetch path must advance by 4 bytes rather than 2. This affects the instruction fetch FIFO/front-end and is triggered by a sequential instruction bus error during an unaligned 32-bit instruction fetch.

title: Fix behavior of exceptions in debug mode, document debug CSRs
body:
This PR consists of three small commits which implement the following changes:
- Exceptions in debug mode shall not modify any CSRs. This resolves #168 and is related to #365.
- Document debug CSRs. This resolves #307.
- Update documentation of `mhartid` CSR. Previously, the doc was still describing the cluster and core ID bit fields.

repo.name: ibex
repo.description: Ibex is a small 32 bit RISC-V CPU core, previously known as zero-riscy.

commits.message:
[rtl] Do not update CSRs upon exceptions in debug mode

In debug mode, exceptions shall not update any CSRs including `mcause`,
`mepc`, `mtval`, `dpc` and `mstatus`, see Debug Spec v0.13.2, p.39.

This resolves lowRISC/ibex#168.

Signed-off-by: Pirmin Vogel <vogelpi@lowrisc.org>

[doc] Document debug CSRs

This resolves lowRISC/ibex#307.

Signed-off-by: Pirmin Vogel <vogelpi@lowrisc.org>

[doc] Update `mhartid` CSR description

This commit removes outdated bit-field descriptions for `mhartid` CSR.

Signed-off-by: Pirmin Vogel <vogelpi@lowrisc.org>

resolved_issues.title: Check behavior of exceptions and special instructions related to debug mode
resolved_issues.body:
Currently, exceptions and special instructions are handled independent of whether the core is in debug mode or not. This is not correct for a couple of cases. For example, the Debug Spec v0.13.2 states on p.39 that while in debug mode:
- ~~WFI acts as a NOP. Currently the core just goes to sleep anyway.~~
- Exceptions do not update any registers such as `mcause`, `mepc`, `mtval`, `dpc` and `mstatus`. Currently, exception handling does not depend on debug mode.

~~Similarly, the DRET instruction must lead to an illegal instruction exception when the core is not in debug mode (p.41). Currently, DRET always restores the PC in dpc even if the core is not in debug mode, thus silently messing up the processor state.~~

resolved_issues.title: Document debug CSRs
resolved_issues.body: Document dscratch0, dscratch1 and dpc CSRs in the CSR documentation, and link them from the debug documentation page.

problem_statement: When Ibex takes an exception while the core is already in Debug Mode, the exception-handling path still overwrites machine Control and Status Registers (CSRs) that record trap state. As a result, `mepc`, `mcause`, `mtval`, and `mstatus` can be modified even though the core is already in Debug Mode. The affected functionality is the Debug Mode exception/CSR handling logic. The correct behavior is that an exception taken in Debug Mode must leave those CSRs unchanged; in particular, it must not clear the interrupt-enable state in `mstatus` or replace the existing trap information in `mepc`, `mcause`, and `mtval`. This is triggered whenever an exception is taken after `debug_mode` is already active.

resolved_issues.body:
Hi all,
I'm executing some tests after booting Ibex into User-Mode, and asserting debug stimulus, and I see the following:
![Screenshot from 2019-11-12 17-28-49](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/16736281/68725023-01090380-0572-11ea-86a8-d11f863ff425.png)
In this test, our debug ROM is located at `0x80004f88`.
We can see that the core's privilege level stays at `PRIV_LVL_U` even after the core has jumped to the debug ROM and `debug_req` has dropped, while the Debug-Mode Spec says that all operation in debug mode should be taken at machine mode. As a result of the current Ibex behavior, illegal instruction exceptions are thrown when we access D-mode CSRs inside of the debug ROM.
However, `dcsr.prv` is being updated properly, and stores the value of `PRIV_LVL_M` after trapping to debug mode, it is just the current privilege mode that is being calculated incorrectly.
Best,
Udi

problem_statement: When Ibex takes a debug request while the core is executing in RISC-V User mode (U-mode), it can jump to the debug ROM while still treating the current execution privilege as U-mode instead of RISC-V Machine mode (M-mode). This affects the debug-entry privilege handling in the core's control and CSR logic. The observed consequence is that code running from the debug ROM can raise illegal-instruction exceptions when it accesses debug control and status registers (CSRs), because those accesses are still being checked as if the core were in U-mode. The expected behavior is that once debug mode is entered, all execution in the debug ROM must run with the core's current privilege level set to M-mode, regardless of the privilege level from which debug was entered.

resolved_issues.title: DMEM fault during misaligned memory access
resolved_issues.body:
Hi all,
When running this set of instructions:
![Screenshot from 2019-10-04 16-43-38](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/16736281/66245995-26c70100-e6c6-11e9-8347-b284c658e62c.png)
The following waves were generated:
![Screenshot from 2019-10-04 16-47-11](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/16736281/66246078-a1901c00-e6c6-11e9-839a-a188fce292f5.png)
The `sw` instructions at `PC=0x800058d0` has a misaligned memory address, and is thus split into two internal memory transactions. In the waves, around 395,800,000ps corresponds to the memory response to the first of these two transactions, which is when the testbench randomly asserts a memory fault here. According to Ibex documentation for this situation, the second memory transaction should continue as normal, ignoring the response data, and then the core needs to also jump to the corresponding fault handler (located at `PC=0x80014000` in our case). The LSU's FSM transitions to it's error handling states from the misaligned transaction states, and the core jumps to `0x80014000` (which encodes the instruction `j 80014080`) directly after `0x800058d0`, but while executing this jump instruction, the core jumps to `0x8001e112` instead, throwing an illegal instruction exception, and then proceeds to wait for the `rvalid` corresponding to the second part of the original misaligned transaction. This occurs around 395,835,000ps, and after this, the core jumps back to the fault handler, and fully executes it. This intermediate PC of `0x8001e112` is calculated as the incorrect jump address from load address data that's already in the execution pipeline, and is muxed through due to `lsu_addr_incr_req_i` going high while waiting for the second half of the misaligned memory transaction to complete. Maybe a potential solution for this would be to only jump to the fault handler after the second part of the misaligned transactions has completed?
Best,
Udi

problem_statement: Recent instruction-side logic and prefetch-buffer changes broke the instruction fetch handshake in Ibex. The instruction-side prefetch buffer issues fetches through a request/grant/response interface: `instr_req_o` requests an instruction fetch, `instr_gnt_i` accepts that request, and the returned instruction data arrives later. In the failing behavior, if a fetch request is made and the grant does not arrive immediately, the prefetch buffer can stop treating that fetch as pending and can advance to a different address before the original request has been accepted. This can desynchronize instruction fetches and cause execution to stop early in the tracing example. The affected logic is the instruction-side prefetch buffer and its request/address tracking. When a fetch is pending but has not yet been granted, including the sequential fetch immediately after a granted branch fetch, `instr_req_o` must remain asserted and `instr_addr_o` must remain at the same word-aligned address until `instr_gnt_i` acknowledges that request.

title: Fix IF stalls preventing deassertion of regfile write enable

repo.description: Ibex is a small 32 bit RISC-V CPU core, previously known as zero-riscy.

commits.message:
ID stage: make single-cycle instr clear `instr_multicycle_done_q`

Previously, this signal was only cleared when starting the next
multi-cycle instruction.

ID stage: only eval `instr_multicycle_done_q` for multi-cycle instr

This signal should only be evaluated if the ID/EX stage currently
executes a multi-cycle instruction. Without this commit, the signal
is also evaluated for single-cycle instructions and can for example
cause the register file write enable to not be de-asserted in case of
stalls in the IF stage.

resolved_issues.title: instr_multicycle_done is not asserted, continuous register writes
resolved_issues.body:
While executing the code shown below:
![Screenshot from 2019-08-05 18-14-11](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/16736281/62504340-e2de7b00-b7ac-11e9-8b26-0cc4090ccec3.png)
We see this incorrect behavior in the core:
![Screenshot from 2019-08-05 18-13-52](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/16736281/62504356-ee31a680-b7ac-11e9-8d28-748683269f7e.png)

As shown, the `addi` instruction at PC `0x80000088` appears to correctly load register `x13` with the value `0xa5a5a5a5`, but at the very next instruction (PC: `0x8000008c`), we can see from the trace log that `x13` now has the value `0xa5a5de17`. 
![Screenshot from 2019-08-05 18-12-33](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/16736281/62504456-76b04700-b7ad-11e9-94ab-524900644a48.png)

From the waveform, `rf_reg[13]` is written correctly by the `addi` after adding the immediate value `0x5a5` (`alu_operand_b_i`), and becomes `0xa5a5a5a5`. After this, the testbench does not assert the `instr_gnt_i` for a number of cycles, leading the core to stay in the DECODE phase while waiting for the next instruction fetch. However, we see that `rf_reg[13]` keeps getting written with the incremented values of `alu_result` in every consecutive cycle that the core waits, as `instr_multicycle_done_q` in the ID stage does not go high after the `addi` finishes. This keeps `regfile_we` at 1, causing the continuous writes.

problem_statement: When a single-cycle instruction such as `addi` completes in Ibex and the next instruction fetch is stalled because the instruction-fetch grant signal (`instr_gnt_i`) stays low, the core can remain in the instruction-decode (ID) stage with the register-file write-enable signal (`regfile_we`) still asserted. During those stalled cycles, the destination register of the completed instruction may be written again even though no new instruction has arrived. The affected functionality is the ID-stage logic that determines when the current instruction has finished and whether register-file writes remain enabled while the instruction-fetch interface is stalled. Once the single-cycle instruction has committed its result, `regfile_we` must be deasserted on every cycle while the core waits for the next instruction-fetch grant, and the destination register must retain its committed value throughout that stall.

title: Rework CSR-related pipeline flushes
body:
This commit clarifies why CSR-related pipeline flushes are needed (e.g. when enabling interrupts), only introduces them when doing the critical modifications (write/set bits in `mstatus` and `mie` CSRs
for enabling interrupts, reads and clears are uncritical for these CSRs), and makes sure the controller is actually able to start handling interrupts while doing a CSR-related pipeline flush.

This resolves lowrisc/ibex#6.

problem_statement: When software uses RISC-V Control and Status Register (CSR) instructions to enable interrupts through the `mie` (machine interrupt-enable) and `mstatus` (machine status) CSRs while an interrupt is already pending, Ibex can perform the CSR-related pipeline flush and then resume normal instruction execution instead of entering the interrupt handler. The failing case is a back-to-back sequence that first enables the relevant source in `mie`, then sets the global interrupt-enable bit in `mstatus`, and then immediately clears that bit again: the pending interrupt can be lost and a following non-interrupt instruction can retire. The affected logic is the CSR-related pipeline-flush and interrupt-entry path around updates to `mie` and `mstatus`. Correct behavior is that once those CSR write/set operations make a pending interrupt eligible for service, the core must take the interrupt before normal execution resumes, even if the next instruction would disable interrupts again.

title: Fix LSU + lint errors
body:
I prepared this PR to get urgent stuff fixed before the bigger changes for the controller and interrupts/exceptions.

This PR contains two commits:
- The first one is a cleanup of the LSU that also fixes a critical error. Previously, misaligned loads/stores were broken as the byte enable generation and read data alignment for the second transaction part were not working. These operations rely on the updated input address having the same alignment as the original address, whereas the LSU provided the aligned output address to the AGU.
- The second one fixes recently introduced linting errors.

Tested using Verilator and Vivado.

repo.name: ibex
repo.description: Ibex is a small 32 bit RISC-V CPU core, previously known as zero-riscy.

commits.message:
LSU cleanup, abort misaligned ops if first part fails

This commit cleans up the LSU and fixes two bugs:

1. If a misalgned transaction creates an error during the first
   part of the transaction, the second part is not pushed out and
   the transaction is aborted. Previously, the LSU tried to output
   also the second part but did not adhere to the defined
   protocol.

2. Misaligned operations are again working correctly. Previously,
   the generation of the byte enable and the alignment of read
   data was broken as these operations rely on the updated
   address from the AGU to have the same alignment as the
   original address.

This partially resolves #121.
Fix linting errors

problem_statement: Ibex mishandles misaligned 32-bit stores in the load-store unit. When a store address is not 32-bit aligned and the access must be split across two adjacent 32-bit words, the address and byte-enable calculation for the second memory transaction is incorrect, so the split store does not preserve the original byte lanes. In the failing boundary case, a 32-bit store to an address whose two least significant bits are `01` is not performed as the required pair of aligned writes. The correct behavior is to issue two aligned store transactions that together write the same four bytes as the original store: the first transaction writes byte lanes 1-3 of the lower word, and the second transaction writes byte lane 0 of the next word. This affects the load-store unit and the address generation used for the second part of a misaligned store, and it is triggered by a misaligned 32-bit store that crosses a 32-bit word boundary.

problem_statement:
## Description
In 32-bit CVA6 configurations, the write-back data cache does not correctly format certain uncacheable stores when the AXI data bus is 64 bits wide. A 32-bit store to an uncacheable memory region can be acknowledged on AXI, but the target peripheral still does not observe the write, so the access appears to be lost.

## Expected Behavior
CVA6 must preserve 32-bit store semantics even when the write-back cache interfaces with a 64-bit AXI data bus. For an uncacheable 32-bit store, the request must be forwarded to AXI as a real write to the target peripheral, with the write data and byte strobes placed on the 32-bit lane selected by the address within the 64-bit AXI beat.

## Actual Behavior
With the write-back cache enabled, the AXI-side formatting for these uncacheable 32-bit stores uses the wrong 32-bit lane. As a result, the AXI transaction is acknowledged, but the write data or strobes are misaligned within the 64-bit beat and the intended peripheral write does not occur.

## Affected Function
The affected logic is the write-back data-cache control path that converts 32-bit CVA6 memory requests into 64-bit AXI write transactions for uncacheable accesses.

## Trigger Condition
This occurs when CVA6 is configured with XLEN=32, the write-back data cache is enabled, the AXI data bus is 64 bits wide, and software performs an uncacheable 32-bit store whose address selects a specific 32-bit lane within the 64-bit AXI beat, including the upper 32-bit half.

problem_statement:
## Description
CVA6 uses a shared translation lookaside buffer (shared TLB) to cache page translations and refill the instruction and data TLBs. The shared TLB lookup can report a hit even when no single cached entry matches the entire request. If one way in a set matches the requested virtual page and a different way matches the requested address-space identifier (ASID), the lookup can incorrectly treat that as a valid hit and return a translation from the wrong address space.

## Expected Behavior
A shared TLB hit is valid only when one cached entry matches all lookup fields for the current request. At minimum, the requested virtual page and the ASID must match in the same entry; if additional virtualization qualifiers are enabled for that translation context, those qualifiers must also match in that same entry. If no single entry satisfies the full lookup, the shared TLB must miss so that CVA6 refills the instruction or data TLB from the correct translation.

## Actual Behavior
The lookup can combine partial matches from different ways in the same set and report a false hit. As a result, CVA6 can return a cached translation even though the ASID of the request does not match the entry that supplied the translation.

## Affected Functionality
Shared TLB hit-detection and tag-match logic in the CVA6 memory-management unit (MMU), specifically the logic that decides whether a cached translation can be used to refill the instruction-side or data-side TLB.

## Trigger Condition
The bug appears when a shared-TLB set contains multiple valid entries with different ASIDs. A concrete failing case is: one way holds virtual page X for ASID 0, another way in the same set holds a different virtual page for ASID 1, and a lookup is performed for virtual page X under ASID 1. That lookup must miss because no single entry matches both X and ASID 1, but the buggy logic can report a hit.

problem_statement:
## Description
In CVA6, the memory management unit (MMU) translates virtual addresses for load and store requests from the load/store unit (LSU). When an LSU request already carries a valid misaligned-address exception, that request should be treated as faulting immediately. Instead, the load/store translation path can still start data-side address translation and produce a page-table memory access for the same request.

## Expected Behavior
If the LSU presents a load or store together with a valid misaligned-address exception, the MMU must return the misaligned exception for that access and stop the translation flow for that request. The same access must not trigger a data-side translation lookup or any page-table memory request.

## Actual Behavior
With load/store address translation enabled, a misaligned LSU request can still initiate translation-side activity and generate an observable page-table memory access even though the request is already being reported as misaligned.

## Affected Function
The affected functionality is the MMU load/store address-translation path, specifically the gating between LSU requests that already carry an exception and the data-side translation/page-table access path.

## Trigger Condition
The bug is triggered when load/store virtual-address translation is enabled and the LSU submits a load or store request that already has a valid misaligned-address exception.

title: Fix a bug that causes the core to freeze when enabling CV-X-IF while disabling RVC extension
body:
This is an attempt to fix the bug described in #3167.

It appears that when enabling the CV-X-IF interface while disabling the RVC extension, the core freezes during the initialization phase of the debug sequence in the testbench.

I managed to find out that this was caused by a bug inside the Decode stage: the compressed‑instruction channel driver of the CV-X-IF inside the Decode stage is only generated if the RVC extension is enabled. However, this module still drives signals inside the stage even when RVC is off. I proposed a fix in the PR below, although I am not sure it is the cleanest way to address the issue.

problem_statement:
## Description
CVA6 can lose forward progress when the CV-X-IF interface for custom extensions is enabled while the RVC extension, the RISC-V compressed-instruction extension, is disabled. In this configuration, the Decode stage can still let the CV-X-IF compressed-instruction path affect instruction decoding even though compressed instructions are not supported. The failure was observed during debug-sequence initialization, where the core freezes instead of continuing execution.

## Expected Behavior
When RVC is disabled, a fetched instruction must be handled as a normal 32-bit uncompressed instruction. Enabling CV-X-IF in that configuration must not block decode, prevent a valid decode result from being issued, change the forwarded 32-bit instruction value, or mark the instruction as compressed.

## Actual Behavior
With CV-X-IF enabled and RVC disabled, the Decode stage may incorrectly let the compressed-instruction path participate in decode. As a result, an ordinary 32-bit instruction can fail to produce a valid issued decode result or be treated as compressed, which causes the core to stop making forward progress.

## Affected Function
Decode-stage handling of the interaction between the normal instruction-decode path and the CV-X-IF compressed-instruction path.

## Trigger Condition
The bug is triggered when CV-X-IF is enabled in a CVA6 configuration that disables RVC, and the core decodes a regular 32-bit instruction, including early instructions seen during debug-sequence initialization.

problem_statement: In Caliptra's KeyVault read client (`kv_read_client`), the status for a multi-beat read transaction can be overwritten by a later beat instead of preserving an earlier failure. If a KeyVault read stays active across multiple beats and one non-final beat reports a read error, a subsequent successful beat, including the final beat, can incorrectly make the overall transaction appear successful. `kv_read_client` is the block that returns KeyVault data to Caliptra hardware consumers. The expected behavior is that once any beat in a read transaction reports a KeyVault read failure, that failure remains latched for the rest of the transaction and the completed read reports failure rather than success.

problem_statement: In Caliptra's Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) engine, software can still rewrite the KeyVault private-key read-control register after an ECC signing operation has started. KeyVault is Caliptra's internal key storage interface used by crypto blocks to fetch protected key material. When ECC signing is configured to use a private key from a KeyVault entry, the selected entry must remain fixed for the entire signing operation. If software writes a different value to the ECC KeyVault private-key control register while the ECC engine is busy, that write should be ignored and the signature should still be generated from the key that was selected before the operation began. Instead, the active KeyVault private-key selection can change mid-operation, which changes the ECC signing result.

problem_statement: In Caliptra 2.0, the VeeR EL2 RISC-V core's AXI4-to-AHB bridge mishandles back-to-back read requests on the load/store path. If one read is followed immediately by another and the AHB-Lite slave deasserts HREADY while the second request is being presented, the bridge can change that second transfer from a valid AHB NONSEQ read to the wrong transfer type and can lose the low address bits of the buffered request. As a result, the second read can appear on AHB at an aligned or otherwise incorrect address instead of the requested address. The correct behavior is to keep the stalled second read as a valid NONSEQ transfer and preserve its exact requested address, including the low address bits, until the AHB slave accepts it.

Bug: ahb_slv_sif continues to assert 'dv' after an error response is received
resolved_issues.body:
This occurs due to the AHB signalling protocol. 
hreadyout is 0 for 1 cycle while hresp = 1. 
Current logic uses hready_i to clear the 'dv' signal or load a new request in from AHB, but that causes pending transactions to be resent on the component interface.

problem_statement: In Caliptra's `ahb_slv_sif` block, which bridges the AMBA Advanced High-performance Bus (AHB) to an internal client request interface, the downstream request-valid signal `dv` remains asserted for one extra clock after an outstanding transfer receives an error response. The bug is triggered when an AHB transfer has already been accepted, the internal client holds the request for at least one cycle, and then the client reports an error during the first AHB error-response cycle while the AHB bus is still not ready. The observed incorrect behavior is that `dv` stays high on that error cycle instead of clearing. The expected behavior is that as soon as the outstanding request completes with an error, `dv` must deassert in that same cycle and remain low until a new valid AHB transfer is accepted.

resolved_issues.title: Simultaneous AXI Read and Write transactions cause incorrect arbitration in subordinate_arb
resolved_issues.body:
The problem happens when the arbiter gets the Read and Write transaction in the same clock cycle. The arbiter is supposed to prioritize Write over Read, however if both of them happen at the same time, the arbiter issues two writes (with the same data) to the underlying logic and the Read is lost.

This issue has been fixed in the i3c-core (which uses the same subordinate AXI arbiter) with https://github.com/chipsalliance/i3c-core/commit/676fc8ed5c38aa4aa61f07988c7dc5303bc03be1

#!/bin/bash
set -e

BASE_SHA="d1a3be59fdadce8169398fd77acc717dc33d282c"

# Stage 1: checkout base_sha in a clean workspace.
cd /home/caliptra-rtl
git reset --hard
git clean -fdx

if ! git cat-file -e "${BASE_SHA}^{commit}" 2>/dev/null; then
  git fetch --depth=1 origin "${BASE_SHA}"
fi

git checkout "${BASE_SHA}"

# Stage 2: sync submodules to the checked-out commit.
git submodule sync --recursive || true
git submodule update --init --recursive || true

# Normalize the one CRLF source file touched by fix.patch so the runtime-mounted
# LF patch applies cleanly inside the harness.
perl -0pi -e 's/\r\n/\n/g' src/integration/rtl/caliptra_top.sv

# Stage 3: detect tool versions from the checked-out repo and align the environment.
verilator_version="v5.044"
riscv_version="v12.1.0"
workflow_file=".github/workflows/build-test-verilator.yml"

if [[ -f "$workflow_file" ]]; then
  detected_verilator="$(awk -F': ' '/^[[:space:]]+VERILATOR_VERSION:/ {gsub(/"/, "", $2); print $2; exit}' "$workflow_file")"
  detected_riscv="$(awk -F': ' '/^[[:space:]]+RISCV_VERSION:/ {gsub(/"/, "", $2); print $2; exit}' "$workflow_file")"
  if [[ -n "$detected_verilator" ]]; then
    verilator_version="$detected_verilator"
  fi
  if [[ -n "$detected_riscv" ]]; then
    riscv_version="$detected_riscv"
  fi
fi

echo "[INFO] Requested Verilator version: ${verilator_version}"
echo "[INFO] Requested RISC-V toolchain version: ${riscv_version}"

if ! command -v verilator >/dev/null 2>&1 || ! verilator --version | head -n1 | grep -q "${verilator_version#v}"; then
  /usr/local/bin/install-verilator-version "${verilator_version}"
fi

if ! command -v riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc >/dev/null 2>&1 || ! riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc --version | head -n1 | grep -q "${riscv_version#v}"; then
  /usr/local/bin/install-caliptra-riscv-toolchain "${riscv_version}"
fi

hash -r

# Stage 4: install minimal Python deps used by the open-source smoke/regression scripts.
python -m pip install -U pip setuptools wheel pyyaml
python -m pip show pyyaml >/dev/null

if [[ ! -f tools/scripts/Makefile ]]; then
  echo "[ERROR] tools/scripts/Makefile not found at ${BASE_SHA}"
  exit 1
fi

verilator --version | head -n1
riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc --version | head -n1
python --version
problem_statement: In Caliptra's AXI subordinate arbiter (`axi_sub_arb`), overlapping read and write traffic can be arbitrated incorrectly when a read request has already been selected but is still blocked by downstream backpressure. If a write request becomes valid in the same cycle that the downstream hold is released, the arbiter can switch to the write too early and the pending read can be lost. This affects the AXI block that merges read and write requests onto a shared downstream request interface. The expected behavior is testable: once a read or write beat has won arbitration, that winner must remain selected until the downstream interface actually accepts that beat; only after the accepted transfer completes may the arbiter apply its normal write-over-read priority to choose the next request. Under this trigger condition, the stalled read must complete first, and the write may be issued only afterward.

problem_statement: In Caliptra's AES control finite-state machine, AES-GCM manual operation is not correctly enforced during the GCM TAG phase. When AES-GCM is configured for manual start, the controller is in the TAG phase, and software has already written a complete input block for tag processing, the block can leave its idle state and begin the GHASH (Galois hash) side of tag handling before software issues the explicit START command. The correct behavior is that manual mode must keep the AES-GCM TAG phase idle until START is asserted; loading the full tag input block alone must not consume that input or begin tag processing. This bug affects the AES subsystem's GCM control path under the trigger condition of manual operation plus a fully loaded TAG-phase input block.

problem_statement: In the Caliptra SHA-512 accelerator, the generate Platform Configuration Register (PCR) hash flow can leave the message-block lock state stuck after the operation finishes. If software runs a generate-PCR-hash command, waits for completion, issues a zeroize, and then starts a normal SHA-512 hash, the SHA-512 block registers can still behave as locked and fail to accept the newly written message block. The following standard SHA-512 command can therefore return an incorrect digest. Zeroize is expected to fully clear any lock state created by the generate-PCR-hash flow so that the next standard SHA-512 command behaves like a fresh operation: newly written block data must be accepted and the digest must match that data. The affected subsystem is the SHA-512 block, specifically the interaction between the generate-PCR-hash path and zeroize recovery.

title: Crypto enhancement
body:
Enhanced crypto modules including:
1) remove deadcode in doe_core_cbc (found by FPV)
dead code in line 254-255 doe_core_cbc.sv:
                    else if(enc_ready)
                        IV_enc_state <= st_IV_engine_idle;

2) froze adder inputs to fix #194 (found by FPV)
With this PR, there is no more constraints on keeping inputs fixed. The only constraint is having a single pulse add_en_i, and do not enable it again until ready_o.

3) remove sca_en_i since countermeasures are hardcoded to be enabled (found by FPV)

4) remove deadcode in ecc_pm_ctrl:163 (found by FPV)
in ecc_pm_ctrl:163 the last else if () is always taken. This PR switches to just else to avoid confusion.

5) Stop faulty ECC from continuing before zeroize (found by FPV): When the error happens for the first time, the error flag goes high and will remain high until zeroize. We expect that uC issues zeroize if there is an error in ECC. In this scenario, although the second command will be performed, the results should not be used since error flag is kept high. However, this PR stops faulty ECC from continuing before zeroize.

6) removed one cycle delay for hmac_drbg ready (found by FPV)
This PR synchronizes hmac_drbg READY to VALID by removing one cycle delay

7) add all_1 protection for LFSR
This PR has protection for the LFSR to stuck to be all 1.

resolved_issues.title: [ECC] add_sub_mod_alter ready not aligned with result
resolved_issues.body:
Hello, 

We found an issue with the ready signal which does not align with the computed result. The expected behaviour of the ready signal is to be set when we have the correct result. In the current implementation the ready arrives 1-2 cycles, if and only if the enable signal is kept low. 

@mojtaba-bisheh confirmed this issue, however, the design works fine with the current implementation, because it does not affect the computation itself. It will be updated in future releases.  

We adde two sets of constraints for this module. One that includes the intended input behaviour and one that fixes the current issues appended with _bugfix. Please remove that constraint after the RTL design updates are done to check for correctness. 

Best
Tobias

problem_statement: In Caliptra's ECC modular add/subtract helper `ecc_add_sub_mod_alter`, a request is not fully captured when `add_en_i` is pulsed. If software or surrounding logic starts an operation with a single-cycle `add_en_i` pulse and then changes `sub_i`, the operands, or the modulus before `ready_o` asserts, the block can raise `ready_o` while `res_o` reflects the newer input values instead of the original transaction. The correct behavior is that each launched operation is self-contained: after a single `add_en_i` pulse, `ready_o` must indicate that `res_o` is valid for the operation mode, operands, and modulus that were present when the request was accepted, and callers should not need to keep those inputs fixed until completion as long as no new operation is issued before `ready_o`.

problem_statement: In Caliptra's `entropy_src` block, the firmware-override observe FIFO overflow indicator is not held in a stable, software-visible state. The observe FIFO is the buffer that lets firmware read raw entropy samples through `FW_OV_RD_DATA`. When firmware override mode is enabled and new entropy samples keep arriving after that FIFO has become full, `FW_OV_RD_FIFO_OVERFLOW` can appear only as a pulse instead of staying asserted. As a result, firmware can miss the fact that samples were dropped and cannot reliably tell whether the data it reads from `FW_OV_RD_DATA` is still a contiguous stream of samples. The expected behavior is that once the firmware-override observe FIFO overflows, `FW_OV_RD_FIFO_OVERFLOW` remains asserted on repeated reads until the observe FIFO has been completely drained and sampling has restarted with contiguous data again; only then should the status clear.

resolved_issues.title: [hmac] `HMAC_CMD_HASH_STOP_BIT` and `HMAC_CMD_HASH_PROCESS` commands causing hang conditions

problem_statement:
## Description
The OpenTitan Hash-based Message Authentication Code (HMAC) IP can hang while finalizing a SHA-256 hash when software writes the last message word into the HMAC message FIFO, waits briefly, and only then issues `HMAC_CMD_HASH_STOP_BIT`, the command that tells the hardware that no more message data is coming. The affected functionality is the SHA-2 finalization path inside the HMAC IP.

## Expected Behavior
After the last message word has been accepted, issuing `HMAC_CMD_HASH_STOP_BIT` after a short delay must still finalize the pending message block, report that the hash operation is complete, and return the HMAC IP to idle. In software-visible terms, the idle bit in `HMAC.STATUS` (`hmac_idle`) must become set again instead of remaining cleared. This must also hold when the message length is exactly one full 512-bit SHA-256 block.

## Actual Behavior
With a short delay between the final FIFO write and `HMAC_CMD_HASH_STOP_BIT`, the hash operation can remain stuck in a non-idle state. Completion is never reported, `HMAC.STATUS.hmac_idle` stays cleared, and software waiting for the HMAC hardware to become idle can block indefinitely.

## Trigger Condition
This occurs when a block-aligned SHA-256 message is written to the HMAC message FIFO, the final 32-bit word completes the last 512-bit block, no further message words are written, and `HMAC_CMD_HASH_STOP_BIT` is issued only after a small delay such as interrupt latency.

resolved_issues.title: [hmac, rtl] Reset hmac_core FSM to Idle after stop
resolved_issues.body:
### Description

I am trying to interleave two HMAC streams. Namely:

- Stream A (HMAC-384) starts and feeds some of its messages.
- Stream A is stopped and the state is saved to SW context.
- Stream B (HMAC-256) starts and feeds some of its messages.
- After around ~1000 bytes or so, Stream B hangs forever, and the initial symptom is MSG_FIFO being full. The test eventually fails with a timeout.

I tried to track down the signals which fetch entries from MSG_FIFO, and I eventually stumbled upon the main FSM of `hmac_core`. When I issue `start` for Stream B, I was expecting `sha_hash_start_o` (of `hmac_core`) signal to be raised, which does not happen.

I am looking at waveforms from a high-level, so I am not sure if it helps much, but here is the clock cycle when `start` command is sent over TL-UL (note the vertical marker). `st_q` of `hmac_core` is at `StMsg` even though HMAC  should have a clear state.
![image](https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/assets/7850700/79d486f6-fd10-42d8-b6b7-624e96957d39)

Maybe we need a condition to go to `Idle` state from `StMsg` state, when `stop` is issued to HMAC HWIP. I do not understand the full interactions here to make a confident suggestion though.  


https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/blob/0e5093d7098daf6b9b848e5c1ca6242336e731d3/hw/ip/hmac/rtl/hmac_core.sv#L352-L370

cc: @martin-velay @gdessouky @andreaskurth

problem_statement:
## Description
During save-and-restore or context-switching use of the OpenTitan HMAC IP, software may stop one HMAC stream, save its state, and then start a different stream. In the reported flow, Stream A is stopped, Stream B is started, and after roughly 1000 bytes Stream B stops making forward progress: the message input FIFO (`MSG_FIFO`) fills and the operation eventually times out. In this failure mode, the HMAC core still behaves as if the previous context is active when the second `start` command arrives.

## Affected Function
The bug is in the HMAC IP's `hmac_core` main state machine, specifically the logic that handles a `stop` request, returns the core to an idle state, and accepts a later `start` during save-and-restore or context-switch flows.

## Expected Behavior
After software issues `stop` for an active HMAC context, the core should finish the current message block, become idle once that block's hash operation completes, and then accept a later `start` for a different context. In that situation, the new `start` must raise the internal `sha_hash_start_o` start pulse and processing of the new stream must begin so that `MSG_FIFO` continues to drain.

## Actual Behavior
If `stop` is issued near the end of a later message block while the first context is still in the inner HMAC message-processing phase, the core may fail to return to its idle state after the current block completes. A subsequent `start` for another context then does not raise `sha_hash_start_o`, so the new stream never actually begins and its `MSG_FIFO` stops draining.

## Trigger Condition
This occurs in HMAC save-and-restore or context-switching flows that stop one stream and start another while the first stream is still processing the inner part of a non-first SHA-2 message block. Reported examples include interleaving HMAC-384 and HMAC-256 streams, and the failure is reproducible in a long SHA-256/HMAC message when `stop` is asserted close to the end of a later block.

problem_statement:
## Description
OpenTitan's CSRNG (Cryptographically Secure Random Number Generator) accepts application commands through per-interface command staging logic (`cmd_stage`). The affected functionality is the CSRNG software application interface (`SW_APP`) command path in this staging logic. An unsupported application-command opcode can be accepted far enough into that path to leave the interface stuck instead of being rejected cleanly.

## Expected Behavior
If `SW_APP` submits an unsupported application command, CSRNG should treat it as a recoverable error without leaving that interface unusable. After the recoverable alert for the invalid request is handled and cleared, a later valid `instantiate` command followed by a valid `uninstantiate` command on the same interface should still complete normally and report successful completion.

## Actual Behavior
An unsupported command can raise the recoverable alert but still leave the `SW_APP` command staging path wedged. After that happens, later legal commands on the same interface may no longer complete as expected. In particular, a normal `instantiate` followed by `uninstantiate` sequence can stop reaching its completion indication even though both commands are valid.

## Trigger Condition
This is triggered when the software application interface receives an unsupported generate-like application command that also carries extra command words, i.e. a nonzero command-length field (`clen`). The failure is especially visible with a multiword invalid request such as the reserved `GENU` opcode with `clen = 2`.

title: [i2c,rtl] Halt controller FSM when unexp. NAK is seen
body:
If the I2C bus NAKs any of our transfers when operating as a Controller-Transmitter in Byte-Formatted Programming Mode, the current behaviour is to proceed to the next FDATA entry as normal, disregarding the NAK entirely. The only side-effect of this event is the block raising the 'nak' interrupt (though this can be suppressed by the use of NAKOK in the FDATA entry).

This PR changes the behaviour so the Controller-FSM halts upon generation of the 'nak' interrupt, and proceeds once the interrupt has been acknowledged using the standard 'Event-Type' interrupt acknowledgement (W1C to INTR_STATE).
The next item in the FMTFIFO is not popped until this acknowledgement is received.
If the NAKOK bit is set for a particular Format Indicator and the bus NAKs our byte, the 'nak' interrupt is not asserted and the FSM continues to the next indicator in the fifo.

While the FSM is halted, SCL is released (we halt in the 'ClockPulseAck' state), and the bus is observed as having an elongated 9th clock period.

Two additional features are also added alongside this change.

- "HOST_NACK_HANDLER_TIMEOUT" CSR
This CSR controls a timeout mechanism where if SW does not handle a pending 'nak'
interrupt before the configured timeout elapses, the hardware will automatically
end the active transaction with a STOP condition and disable Host-Mode.

- "STATUS.HOST_DISABLED_NACK_TIMEOUT" bit
This bit is set when the block times out with the "HOST_NACK_HANDLER_TIMEOUT"
mechanism, and clears when SW re-enables Host-Mode. This is intended to inform
software that the timeout occurred.

The I2C agent / infrastructure does not currently support the generation of NAK's when operating as a Target-Receiver, so this PR also adds rudimentary support for this with a new Agent sequence, plus a test to exercise it (`i2c_host_may_nack`). The testbench currently models the SW interrupt handler latency with a fixed 1000-cycle delay. This should be expanded in the future.

TODO

- [x] Update documentation
- [ ] Check & Update TLTs

---

This new behaviour will need more comprehensive testing to achieve V2 quality. Our infrastructure to test this is currently incomplete, and will need to be expanded. I have observed some of the expected behaviour in an ad-hoc simulation, but it should not be considered fully robust until further testing is completed.

---

Closes #18917

+
+// I2C Agent sequence which behaves as an I2C TARGET.
+//
+// - Receives seq_items from req_analysis_fifo which are sent onto the driver.
+// - If the item is requesting to drive an ACK, 50/50 to change this to a NACK instead.

+class i2c_target_may_nack_seq extends i2c_base_seq;
+  `uvm_object_utils(i2c_target_may_nack_seq)
+  `uvm_object_new
+
+  virtual task body();
+    case (cfg.if_mode)
+      Device: send_device_mode_txn();
+      Host:    `uvm_fatal(`gfn, "This sequence is for the agent in TARGET-Mode only!")
+      default: `uvm_fatal(`gfn, "Invalid cfg.if_mode!")
+    endcase
+  endtask : body
+
+  virtual task send_device_mode_txn();
+    bit [7:0] rdata;
+    forever begin
+      p_sequencer.req_analysis_fifo.get(req);
+      // If it's a read type response, create randomized return data
+      if (req.drv_type == RdData) begin
+        `DV_CHECK_STD_RANDOMIZE_FATAL(rdata)
+        req.rdata = rdata;
+      end
+      // Convert some of the 'DevAck' items from the monitor into NACKs
+      if (req.drv_type == DevAck) begin
+        if ($urandom_range(0, 1)) begin
+          `uvm_info(`gfn, "Converting an ACK to a NACK!", UVM_LOW)
+          req.drv_type = DevNack;
+        end
+      end
+      start_item(req);
+      finish_item(req);
+    end
+  endtask
+

+#### Halt-on-NAK
+
+If the Host-Mode Controller-Transmitter transmits a byte and the 9th bit is a NACK from the Target/Bus, the `nak` interrupt is usually asserted (modulo the effect of [`FDATA.NAKOK`](registers.md#fdata)).
+If the 'nak' interrupt is asserted, the Byte-Formatted Programming Mode FSM will halt until the interrupt has been acknowledged using the standard 'Event-Type' interrupt acknowledgement (W1C to INTR_STATE).
+Software will likely want to do one of two things in handling this irq:
+1. End the current transaction by setting [`CTRL.ENABLEHOST`](registers.md#ctrl) to `1'b0`, and clear the FIFOs ready to begin a new transaction.
+2. Clear the FIFOs, then begin a new transfer without ending the transaction by add new FDATA indicators to the FMTFIFO.
+   In this case, the first entry written to the FMTFIFO should have [`FDATA.START`](registers.md#fdata) set to `1'b1` to create a repeated start condition.
+
+While the FSM is halted, SCL/SDA are released and the bus is observed as having an elongated 9th clock period.
+
+The Halt-on-'NAK' behaviour may be problematic if SW is not responsive, so there is a timeout mechanism that can automatically end the transaction by creating a STOP condition and disabling Host-Mode.
+This is configured using the [`HOST_NACK_HANDLER_TIMEOUT`](registers.md#host_nack_handler_timeout) CSR, which allows software to configure the delay before hardware will terminate the transaction.
+Hardware will also automatically clear [`CTRL.ENABLEHOST`](registers.md#ctrl) when this occurs.
+If this mechanism activates, software can be informed by reading the [`STATUS.HOST_DISABLED_NACK_TIMEOUT`](registers.md#status) bit.
+This field is cleared when software next activates Host-Mode by setting [`CTRL.ENABLEHOST`](registers.md#ctrl) to `1'b1`.
+Before re-activating Host-Mode, software should ensure that the 'nak' interrupt has been handled and acknowledged.

problem_statement:
## Description
The OpenTitan I2C IP mishandles an unexpected negative acknowledgment (NACK) in host mode when it is acting as a controller-transmitter in Byte-Formatted Programming Mode, where software queues host format commands in the format FIFO through FDATA entries. If the target acknowledges the address byte but then NACKs a transmitted data byte, the controller records the NACK but can still advance to the next queued format entry instead of pausing at the failed byte.

## Expected Behavior
After an unexpected NACK in this host-mode transmit path, the I2C controller must stop consuming additional FDATA / format FIFO entries and keep the active transaction paused until software clears the pending `nak` interrupt. While the NACK is pending, the controller must remain in an active host transaction rather than returning to host-idle state, and queued format entries must remain in the FIFO instead of being drained.

## Actual Behavior
The current implementation raises the `nak` interrupt but continues processing the queued transfer. In the reproduced case where the address phase is ACKed and the first queued data byte is NACKed, later queued bytes can still be consumed and the transfer can continue before software clears the interrupt.

## Affected Function
This affects the OpenTitan I2C IP's host-mode byte-formatting controller finite state machine (FSM), specifically the logic that handles ACK/NACK results after transmitting a byte and decides whether to pop the next format FIFO entry.

## Trigger Condition
The bug is triggered when the I2C block is operating in host mode as a controller-transmitter, software has queued multiple FDATA entries for a write transaction, the target acknowledges the address byte, and the target then NACKs the first queued data byte before software has cleared the pending NACK condition.

title: [rtl,pwrmgr] Fix escalation timeout persistence
body:
The escalation timeout needs to persist until reset. The timeout is detected by clk_i, but the timeout is used to drive a flop clocked by clk_lc. This change adds a synchronizer from clk_i to clk_lc, and a clk_lc flop reset by rst_lc_n. The output of this flop is used to set the fault_status and as a reset request.

Fixes #20516

commits.message:
[rtl,pwrmgr] Fix escalation timeout persistence

The escalation timeout needs to persist until reset. The timeout is detected by
clk_i, but the timeout is used to drive a flop clocked by clk_lc. This change
adds a synchronizer from clk_i to clk_lc, and a clk_lc flop reset by rst_lc_n.
The output of this flop is used to set the fault_status and as a reset request.

With this fix the pwrmgr_escalation_reset test passes at the block level.

Fixes #20516

Signed-off-by: Guillermo Maturana <maturana@opentitan.org>

resolved_issues.title: [rtl,pwrmgr] escalation timeout should persist
resolved_issues.body:
### Description

If the escalation network stops for more than 128 cycles, pwrmgr should request an escalation reset, per https://opentitan.org/book/hw/top_earlgrey/ip_autogen/pwrmgr/doc/theory_of_operation.html#escalation-clock-timeout.

However, the escalation timeout condition (esc_timeout in pwrmgr.sv) does not persist, unlike esc_rst_req_d/q. This means if the escalation clock restarts soon after 128 cycles of being inactive an escalation reset won't be generated.

One simple fix would be to flop esc_timeout, similar to how esc_rst_req_d is treated.

#!/bin/bash
set -u -o pipefail

cd /home/opentitan || exit 1
export PATH="/tools/riscv/bin:/tools/verible/bin:$PATH"

TEST_NAME="pwrmgr_escalation_timeout_persist"
TB_ROOT="/home/opentitan/.tb_pwrmgr_escalation_timeout"
SCRATCH_ROOT="${TB_ROOT}/scratch"
LOG_PATH="${TB_ROOT}/dvsim.log"

emit_result() {
  local status="$1"
  echo "HWE_BENCH_RESULTS_START"
  echo "TEST: ${TEST_NAME} ... ${status}"
  echo "HWE_BENCH_RESULTS_END"
}

mkdir -p "${TB_ROOT}"
rm -rf "${SCRATCH_ROOT}"

python - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path

paths = [
    Path("hw/top_earlgrey/ip_autogen/pwrmgr/dv/env/seq_lib/pwrmgr_escalation_timeout_vseq.sv"),
    Path("hw/ip_templates/pwrmgr/dv/env/seq_lib/pwrmgr_escalation_timeout_vseq.sv"),
]
old = "    // check_stopped_esc_clk(136, 1'b1);\n"
new = "    check_stopped_esc_clk(136, 1'b1);\n"

for path in paths:
    text = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    if new in text:
        continue
    if old not in text:
        raise SystemExit(f"marker not found in {path}")
    path.write_text(text.replace(old, new, 1), encoding="utf-8")
PY
prep_rc=$?
if [[ ${prep_rc} -ne 0 ]]; then
  emit_result "FAIL"
  exit "${prep_rc}"
fi

set +e
timeout 1800 ./util/dvsim/dvsim.py \
  hw/top_earlgrey/ip_autogen/pwrmgr/dv/pwrmgr_sim_cfg.hjson \
  -i pwrmgr_escalation_timeout \
  -t vcs \
  --local \
  --fixed-seed 2 \
  --build-seed 1 \
  --scratch-root "${SCRATCH_ROOT}" \
  --purge \
  --max-parallel 1 \
  --build-timeout-mins 20 \
  --run-timeout-mins 10 \
  --no-rerun \
  -v m \
  2>&1 | tee "${LOG_PATH}"
rc=${PIPESTATUS[0]}
set -e

if [[ ${rc} -eq 0 ]]; then
  emit_result "PASS"
else
  emit_result "FAIL"
fi
exit "${rc}"

problem_statement:
## Description
OpenTitan's Power Manager (pwrmgr) contains escalation clock-timeout logic that is supposed to detect when the alert escalation path stops responding while the system is in its normal active state. If the escalation clock remains inactive for more than 128 pwrmgr clock cycles, pwrmgr must treat that as an escalation fault and initiate a local escalation reset.

## Expected Behavior
A stall shorter than the 128-cycle timeout threshold must not trigger an escalation reset. Once the escalation clock has been inactive long enough to exceed that threshold, the timeout condition must persist until reset handling takes effect. Even if the escalation clock starts toggling again shortly after the threshold is crossed, pwrmgr must still disable CPU fetch and issue the escalation reset request.

## Actual Behavior
The timeout condition is not persistent. If the escalation clock stops for only slightly more than the timeout threshold and then restarts soon afterward, pwrmgr can lose the fault indication before the reset path reacts to it. In that case, CPU fetch remains enabled and no escalation reset request is generated even though the timeout threshold was exceeded.

## Trigger Condition
This bug is triggered in the pwrmgr escalation timeout path when the escalation clock is halted just over the 128-cycle limit and then restarted before the fault has been latched as a persistent reset condition. Very long stalls still trigger the reset reliably, so the failure is most visible in near-threshold cases.

title: [mbx] Improve Abort handling, and recovery from communications failure.
body:
This PR implements a FW-initiated reset of the Inbound and Outbound data paths in the event of a communications failure within the SoC<->mailbox<->TL-UL chain and improves the Abort handling.

_Mailbox operation is critical to all communication between the SoC and RoT, and use of the asynchronous reset of the IP block is considered infeasible because it is common to many other IP blocks._


The logic is currently reliant upon everything completing as expected (whether successfully or by an error being indicated by the TL-UL device/bus), but is not robust against potential design flaws nor against any reliability issues with the specific physical device. Further, the current Error and Abort handling mechanisms do not have the capacity to reset fully the internal state of the mailbox logic. ([Issue detailed here](https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan-integrated/issues/708).)

To help with understanding this PR, the Abort mechanism is described below:

- in the event of a failure in the Request/Response mechanism, the SoC side has the capacity to request that an operation be Aborted and it is expected that this mechanism be used in response to a communications timeout (of the order of > 1 second).
- the Abort request is signaled to the RoT via an interrupt.
- the RoT firmware acknowledges the Abort condition.

It is worth noting that the SoC side itself may become stalled and unable to employ the Abort mechanism, since a Write Data access from the SoC when sending the Request may cause the SoC to be blocked upon completion of the previous write. Similarly, a Read Data access from the SoC when fetching the Response will block until the read data is retrieved from the mailbox SRAM.

It is therefore proposed that the Abort acknowledgment should be available as a RoT FW-initiated reset of the mailbox logic, for use even if there has been no explicit Abort request from the SoC side.

This PR consists of two commits:

**Commit 1:** Introduces a reset of the following internal state when the RoT FW ('host') acknowledges an Abort condition.

- u_ombx.u_req_state <- TL-UL read request
- u_ombx.u_pop_entry <- ditto
- u_ombx.u_pending <- SoC side Write Data Register stall
- u_imbx.u_req_state <- TL-UL write request
- u_imbx.u_pending <- ditto

It also clears down the count of outstanding TL-UL bus requests (`u_sramrwarb.u_outstanding_req_cnt`) and suppresses any subsequent TL-UL read response from being propagated into the Outbound mailbox logic, because that previously would result in the logic re-entering an active state as if starting to send a fresh Response to the SoC side.

**Commit 2:** Prioritizes the host-side Abort acknowledgement over all FSM states such that it may be used as a FW-initiated reset at any time, and not just when handling an explicit Abort request from the SoC. This would be used after a timeout in the communications from/to the SoC side. (Apologies: This changes the FSM identation and confuses diff tools.)

This should address [issue 708](https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan-integrated/issues/708) although DV is currently unable to verify the existing Abort handling or the complete efficacy of this change. The smoke test still passes as expected.

commits.message:
[mbx] Fault recovery via Abort mechanism

Clearing of Abort condition resets both inbound and outbound
traffic, clears down the count of outstanding requests and
suppresses any subsequent core-side TL-UL read responses.
Since the Abort request clears Ready, keep the Read Data
register zeroed until the abort is acknowledged.

Signed-off-by: Adrian Lees <a.lees@lowrisc.org>

[mbx] Abort acknowledgement always resets FSMs.

Abort acknowledgement is of the highest priority, permitting
its use as a FW-driven reset mechanism even if there was no
explicit SoC-side Abort request.

Signed-off-by: Adrian Lees <a.lees@lowrisc.org>

resolved_issues.title: [hmac] Revise localparams to have unique and meaningful names
resolved_issues.body:
The issue #701 is reported by @imphil

Problem:

    Previous version of `hmac_pkg.sv` has duplicated names `k`. `k` is
    used as localparam and also used as an argument in `compress()`
    function.

The `k` in localparam is the first 32bit of fractional part for the
cubic root of the first 64 primes. So the name is changed to have the
meaning.

problem_statement:
## Description
OpenTitan's mailbox (mbx) IP carries request and response traffic between the SoC and the Root of Trust (RoT). The inbound mailbox accepts request data written by the SoC, and the outbound mailbox presents response data for the SoC to read. After a communication failure or timeout on this path, RoT firmware must be able to acknowledge the abort condition and use that acknowledgement as a firmware-driven reset of the mailbox control logic, even when the SoC cannot complete the normal abort handshake first.

## Affected Function
The affected logic is the mbx IP's inbound and outbound mailbox control state machines, including the outbound Ready indication during abort recovery.

## Expected Behavior
When RoT firmware acknowledges the abort condition, the mailbox must immediately return to its idle state regardless of which mailbox FSM state is currently active. This must work while the inbound mailbox is already in its write phase and while the outbound mailbox is already in its read/response phase. For an outbound transaction, the same abort acknowledgement must also clear the Ready indication for the aborted response. After that reset, the mailbox must be able to start a new inbound or outbound transaction normally.

## Actual Behavior
In the current implementation, an abort acknowledgement from RoT firmware is not honored once the mailbox FSM has already left idle. If the inbound mailbox is already accepting write data, or the outbound mailbox is already in its read/response phase, the FSM can remain in its active state instead of returning to idle. On the outbound side, Ready can also remain asserted for an aborted response. As a result, the aborted transaction is not fully cleared and the mailbox does not reliably recover for the next transaction.

## Trigger Condition
This bug is triggered when a mailbox transaction is already active and RoT firmware acknowledges the abort condition during recovery from a communication failure or timeout. It also occurs when that acknowledgement is used as a firmware-driven reset without a preceding SoC-side abort request, which is needed when the SoC is stalled and cannot complete the explicit abort sequence.

title: [edn] Clear auto cmd FIFOs after edn disable
body:
This PR clears the auto cmd FIFOs after the edn is disabled.
For more precise information check out the individual commit messages.

This PR resolves #19653

repo.name: opentitan
repo.description: OpenTitan: Open source silicon root of trust

commits.message:
[edn] Reset auto cmd FIFOs when EDN is disabled

This commit resets the auto mode cmd FIFOs whenever the EDN is disabled.
This is done by setting the main_sm_done_pulse_o to high whenever the
edn_enable_i signal changes to low. In edn_core.sv, the done_pulse is used
for several purposes other than just resetting the FIFOs. However, this change
has no or little impact for the other three use cases of this signal. In two of
those three cases the done_pulse has no impact, since the EDN is disabled and the
multiplexer ignores the pulse. In the third case the max_num_between_reseeds is
loaded into a counter whenever the done_pulse is high. This should be fine since the
CSRNG is initialized anyways, should the EDN enter auto mode at a later time.
The only difference for the third case would be that when the auto mode is left
through disabling the EDN, the counter is now reset and should it re-enter auto
mode the counter starts counting from 0 again. This didn't use to be the case.

Signed-off-by: Hakim Filali <hfilali@lowrisc.org>

[edn] Get the DV environment in line with resetting FIFOs after EDN is disabled

This commit gets the DV environment in line with the prior change. This includes
waiting for the EDN to be enabled before disabling in edn_disable_auto_req_mode_vseq.
It also includes an update for the tracing of the scoreboard FIFOs.

Signed-off-by: Hakim Filali <hfilali@lowrisc.org>

[edn/doc] Update documentation to explain when auto cmd FIFOs are cleared

This commit updates the documentation to make it more clear when exactly
the auto command FIFOs are cleared.

Signed-off-by: Hakim Filali <hfilali@lowrisc.org>

resolved_issues.title: [edn] Discussion on Generate/Reseed cmd FIFOs behavior when disabling EDN
resolved_issues.body:
### Description

Currently the Reseed_cmd and the Generate_cmd FIFOs get cleared whenever the CTRL. CMD_FIFO_RST flag is set to true or when the edn_main_sm generates a done pulse. A done_pulse is generated on 3 different occasions:

1. Then edn_main_sm transitions from the BootPulse to the BootDone state (in boot_req_mode)
2. The edn_main_sm transitions from the AutoDispatch to the Idle state (when auto_req_mode is disabled)
3. The edn_main_sm transitions from the Idle state to the sw_port_mode state (when boot/auto_req_mode are both disabled)

The FIFOs aren't cleared however, when the EDN is disabled. E.g. the transition from the AutoDispatch to the Idle state could also happen when the EDN is disabled. In that case, the FIFOs aren't cleared. Even though it has the same initial and final state as point 2.

We should discuss if this is the intended behavior. And if not, when do we want to clear the FIFOs?

The results of this discussion should be added to the documentation.

FYI: @vogelpi @andreaskurth
